extracted.intended_audience: staff at community colleges and nonprofit organizations preparing grant proposals (grant writers, program directors, development officers)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical, step-by-step guidance for researching, organizing, writing, budgeting, evaluating, and packaging grant proposals and inquiry letters for public and private funders. Emphasizes proposal components, funder differences, and presentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characteristics of government funding
rubrics_metrics.description: Government (federal, state, local) grant programs are available to nonprofit organizations but have particular characteristics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is a slow process; there are reduced grant programs through government agencies; there are specific grant deadlines and specific procedures for review; grant program priorities and funding levels are determined each year by Congress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sources for locating government funding
rubrics_metrics.description: Primary publications and methods to find federal, state and local funding opportunities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Federal: Federal Register (notices of funding availability); Commerce Business Daily (primarily federal contracts). State: Kansas Register or equivalent. Local: monitor by telephone, personal contact or letter; stay acquainted with local agencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characteristics of foundation giving
rubrics_metrics.description: How private foundations operate and what drives their grantmaking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Foundation giving is based on established priorities; foundations accept proposals and decide by governing board approval; funding often is one-time. Foundations are regulated by IRS; many kinds exist (family, corporate-sponsored, community, special purpose).

rubrics_metrics.name: Classifications of foundations
rubrics_metrics.description: Different types of private foundations and how they differ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Family/Independent foundations (majority; board often relatives); Corporate/company-sponsored foundations (funded by a corporation but legally independent); Community foundations (city-wide pooled funds with broad boards); Special purpose foundations (fund narrow interests). Use these classifications when researching fit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characteristics and uniqueness of corporate giving
rubrics_metrics.description: Features of corporate philanthropy and how to approach corporations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Visibility is important; giving follows corporate fiscal year; a budget set aside for new projects may exist; corporate giving is not always through PR; proximity to the corporation helps; corporate giving is often evaluated in business terms. Corporations can give cash, in-kind support, employee time/energy; only ~20% of corporations give, indicating potential opportunity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civic groups as funding sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Local civic and service organizations as potential funders or volunteers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rotary, Lions, women's groups, churches provide funds/time. Compile names annually. Seek speaking slots or presentations to solicit support. Contributions vary from endowments to volunteer help or underwriting special events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Individual donor characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: How and why individuals give and where to find prospects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Individual contributors provide the majority of philanthropic dollars; gifts range widely. Individuals give to causes they care about, with matching objectives and where they receive personal attention. Potential donors can be identified from Who's Who, social registers, arts organization lists, newspapers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differences between public and private funding proposals
rubrics_metrics.description: Key contrasts that affect proposal length, form, deadlines, writing style, and budget detail depending on funder type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public funding: usually very long, always has forms (cover forms, budget pages, charts), always deadlines (one-time), bureaucratic/professional/formal writing, budget usually limited to the program requested. Private funding: often starts with a 1–2 page inquiry letter, fewer forms (2–4 pages if any), fewer formal deadlines, more general/journalistic writing, may request organizational annual budgets and audits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposal as an instrument of persuasion
rubrics_metrics.description: A proposal must present a future program clearly and convince funders of its merit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe chronological activities, individuals, organizations and funds necessary. Persuade the reader that the program is essential to the target population; well-planned and logical; competently staffed; producing significant benefits; supported by community or partners; and cost-effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of grants (definitions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Common grant categories to match your request to funder priorities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Program grant (services), equipment grant (special equipment), training grant (education/training), planning grant (planning/coordination), research grant (study/evaluation). Use appropriate category when targeting funders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of proposals (inquiry letter vs full proposal)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two common submission formats and when to use each.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most private funders want a 2–3 page inquiry/proposal letter first; many funders (especially public) require a full-blown proposal with detailed sections and forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overview of the proposal development process
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommended sequential steps for researching, writing, revising, and submitting a grant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify funding source; research and obtain guidelines; read for points of emphasis; develop work plan and outline; brainstorm ideas and budget; perform research; organize ideas; write draft and budget; assemble attachments; pencil in forms; review/edit with multiple reviewers; review against guidelines; rewrite and edit; type final forms and copy; proofread; write summary/cover letter/T.O.C.; package grant; submit by deadline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Writing style and tone consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: How to choose and maintain voice and person throughout the proposal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Style and tone are established in the first section and must be followed throughout for consistency. Prefer third person institutionalized style for formal proposals unless a funder prefers an informal style. If using first/second person, remain informal throughout.

rubrics_metrics.name: Getting organized: know your audience and goals
rubrics_metrics.description: Preparation before writing: clarify purpose, audience, and desired results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask: Who will review this grant? Why are you writing it? What results do you want? What questions should the program answer? Identify activities involved. Methods to capture ideas: start-up sheet, Post-It notes, outline, brainstorming, index cards. Do background research and record sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Program design development (planning with stakeholders)
rubrics_metrics.description: How to convene and run planning meetings to develop the program design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hold a small efficient meeting of principals; review guidelines and discuss each major section; designate a note taker/tape session. Answer: what will the program do; who will operate it; when will it run; who is served (numbers/characteristics); what are objectives; costs; location; significance; why money is needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposal/inquiry letter components
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommended outline and required content for a 2–3 page proposal or inquiry letter to private funders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include: Summary (WHO, WHERE, WHY, WHAT, WHEN, HOW MUCH); Background information on organization (what it is, functions, who uses services, where located); Needs (why funding is needed, what can be done with funds); Description of fundraising project (what, when, results, cost); Fundraising plan (where/when/from whom); Request (exact amount requested); List of attachments (board members, budget, brochure, letters of support, architectural drawings if relevant). Keep letter brief, concise, organized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduction and organizational capability statement
rubrics_metrics.description: What to include in the opening section that establishes organizational credibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State purpose and mission; number of years in operation or reason for new organization; successes and history; staff description; community resources; references to credibility; size of clientele; publications; major accomplishments; important events; and supportive quotes or letters. Spend time enhancing credibility here rather than over-describing the program.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statement of problem / need
rubrics_metrics.description: How to define and document the problem your project addresses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limit to the problem the proposed project will address; present demographic and statistical data that document and support need; be concise; do not write general unsubstantiated statements. Use charts/graphs/maps to strengthen statistical presentation. Describe limitations of existing programs and how your project complements or fills gaps. Include evidence of demand (surveys, community reports) and references for statistical sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantitative documentation (use of statistics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Standards for presenting numeric evidence to support need and claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use specific statements of fact rather than generalities. Example contrasts provided: general 'many students at risk' vs specific percent and numbers and causes. Present statistics concisely and cite sources. Use tables/graphs when helpful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Goals and objectives (distinguish and write correctly)
rubrics_metrics.description: How to state project goals (broad) and measurable objectives (specific outcomes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Goals: few (preferably ≤5), abstract, long-term, not measurable. Objectives: specific, measurable, short-term, outcome-focused (start with verbs like 'to increase', 'to reduce') and state who will do what and how much. Avoid phrasing objectives as methods ('to provide', 'to establish'). Break objectives into activities/action steps and place on a timeline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Project methodology / implementation
rubrics_metrics.description: What to include when describing how the project will be carried out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe the approach and plan of action in detail, link objectives to the plan, explain participant selection, day-to-day operations, and cooperating organizations. Make clear how the program will operate and how activities achieve objectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personnel, organizational structure and staffing patterns
rubrics_metrics.description: How to present staffing, roles, and credentials to reviewers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include organizational chart if requested; describe board and committees; explain staffing pattern and level of effort for each position (percentage/time); list duties and qualifications of staff who will perform the work; include job descriptions and resumes for key personnel in the appendix.

rubrics_metrics.name: Results and benefits (short- and long-term outcomes)
rubrics_metrics.description: What to report about expected program impact and contributions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe number of people to be served; new products produced; problems addressed; future consequences of project; community/state/regional/national impact; and contribution to field, policy, practice, research, or theory. Be specific about measurable benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Future funding / sustainability plan
rubrics_metrics.description: How to address funders’ concern about ongoing support after grant period ends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most foundations expect a plan for sustaining the program. Explain how the program will be funded post-grant (fees for service, other funders, fundraising campaign) and document any expressions of interest from other funders. Provide annual operating budgets, audits, and investment/property information if requested.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation requirements and design
rubrics_metrics.description: What funders expect in an evaluation section and how to design it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most funders require evaluation. Decide whether you will do a program evaluation (did it achieve objectives and can outcomes be attributed to program) or a process evaluation (was program implemented as planned and what is the relationship of activities to effectiveness). Prefer an external evaluator for objectivity. Cover cost, evaluator selection and credentials, their participation in designing evaluation, evaluation criteria, data-gathering methods, test instruments/questionnaires, data analysis, how results will be used to improve program, and schedule of evaluation reports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Budget standards (specificity, detail, accuracy)
rubrics_metrics.description: General expectations for building a fundable budget.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Budget must be specific, detailed, informative and contain correct arithmetic. Include an income budget listing all sources and an expense budget itemizing personnel, fringe, consultants, space, equipment, supplies, travel, other costs and indirect costs as applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expense budget categories and calculation guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: How to itemize and compute typical budget line items.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Personnel: list individual staff, monthly salary x % time x months. Fringe: list each fringe benefit and percentage of salaries. Consultants: list individually with hours/days x fee x occurrences. Space costs: itemize square footage x price per unit. Equipment: list each item x quantity x unit cost. Supplies: list usage x price or price per month x months. Travel: separate in-state (mileage) and out-of-state (airfare + lodging + per diem) with calculation examples. Other costs: telephone, postage, printing, materials. Provide examples and show arithmetic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indirect costs
rubrics_metrics.description: Treatment and presentation of overhead/indirect costs in a budget.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indirect costs are estimated as a negotiated percentage applied typically to salaries and fringe; they represent organizational operating costs (building, maintenance, general salaries, accounting). Negotiate indirect cost rate ahead of time with funder and disclose how it is calculated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Budget narrative
rubrics_metrics.description: Explanatory narrative that accompanies a budget to justify items.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always include a budget narrative placed behind the budget. Explain why people are paid certain rates, why travel is needed, and justify major line items so reviewers understand the rationale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cover letter (letter of transmittal) requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Required content and tone for the transmittal cover letter that accompanies a proposal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include name of organization; concise summary of proposed program/study; amount requested; brief statement of interest and capability to perform the project; contact name/address/phone/title for follow-up; sign on organization stationery by CEO or Board Chair; keep brief and designate a contact person.

rubrics_metrics.name: Title page requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Elements that should appear on a proposal title page when funder does not supply one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include title of proposal; agency/organization receiving the proposal; the program under which submitted; name, address, phone of proposer (and organization name); date of submission. For federal/state/local funders, fill out required cover/title pages as provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Table of contents formatting and use
rubrics_metrics.description: When and how to include a table of contents in a proposal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a separate page for T.O.C. when proposal is >10 pages or contains many attachments. Present formal outline with Roman numerals for major headings, capital letters for subheads, Arabic numbers for sections, and lower-case letters for subsections. Include page numbers and list graphs/tables/attachments. Headings must appear exactly as they do in the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive summary / proposal summary
rubrics_metrics.description: Purpose, length, and content expectations for the summary or abstract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Long proposals (>5–10 pages): include a one-page summary/abstract that answers Who? What? When? Why? Where? How Much? Write the summary last. Short proposals (1–5 pages): make the first paragraph the summary. The summary must be well-written and set the tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forms handling best practices
rubrics_metrics.description: How to prepare and submit required application forms accurately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make a copy of forms for drafting; review answers carefully; do not type final forms until draft has been thoroughly proofed and edited. Submit originals if possible to ensure neatness and accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attachments and appendix contents
rubrics_metrics.description: Types of supporting documents to include in an appendix and where to place them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include annual reports, charts/graphs, publications/studies pertinent to the project, references, list of Board of Directors, contracts, operating budget sheets, letters of support, job descriptions, organizational chart, resumes, and architectural renderings when relevant. Place attachments behind narrative in the appendix.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editing process and checklist
rubrics_metrics.description: How to edit and a checklist of presentation and content quality items to verify before submission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not try to write and edit simultaneously. Complete a full draft then edit. Checklist items: clarity (facts clearly stated; minimal jargon); clear explanations (make a clear request for action); readability (suit audience); completeness (all necessary data included); presentation (principal idea highlighted; logical order; flow); appropriate tone (friendly/personal/formal as required); visual attractiveness (spacing, uncluttered); paragraph and sentence length; error-free (spelling, grammar, punctuation); accuracy (facts/statistics verified); consistency (point of view clear); positive approach (upbeat/confident).

rubrics_metrics.name: Packaging and visual presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Physical presentation considerations to make the proposal easy and pleasant to read.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use generous white space; consistent margins; consider whether to justify right-hand margin; use readable type (avoid script and dot-matrix); ensure printer quality is at least letter-quality; avoid widowed/orphaned single lines at top of pages; follow funder instructions on covers or binding (staple vs binder).

rubrics_metrics.name: Submission timing and deadline compliance
rubrics_metrics.description: Meeting funder deadlines and schedule constraints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public funding programs always have deadlines and scheduled submission windows; private funders may accept proposals anytime but may also have cycles. Plan backward from deadlines and submit by the required date.
